side-32.title: The Weight of One Tablet
side-32.summary: I only woke up at noon.
beats: One: The First Day Off the Pills
I only woke up at noon.

The curtains weren't fully closed; light came in through the gap and fell at the foot of the bed. Doudou was crouched at the door, tail drumming the floor. I bought him two months ago — a very small brown dog.
He didn't know I couldn't get up. He only knew I'd promised to take him out.
Doudou carried the leash over and put it by my bed. I reached out and touched his head. I didn't get up.
I tried to sit up. My legs were soft. Not pain — they just wouldn't move. Like paper soaked through with water.
The phone rang by the pillow. Message after message in the work group; someone asking about a report. I typed a few words, then deleted them.
Someone posted a meme in the work group. I stared at it for a long time before remembering I was supposed to reply. Mom sent a voice message, asking if I wanted to come home for dinner this weekend.
I didn't reply. I wanted to, but I didn't know what to say.
There was no specific bad thing. Mom is very accepting of me. Nothing major happened at home. But I was just sad, anxious — like something in my chest was slowly leaking.
Doudou's bowl was empty. I got up and poured him some kibble. He ate loudly. I stood in the kitchen and felt very far from the sound.
I weighed myself. Forty-five kilos.
I didn't tell anyone.
I went back to bed and stared at the ceiling. Then I took the smallest piece.
An hour later, Doudou became very cute. The messages in the work group weren't so scary. Mom's voice came out of the phone like she really did love me.
I even thought I could take Doudou to the park tomorrow.
I knew it was wrong. But in that hour, I felt like a normal person.
Not 'happy' — 'normal'. Able to get up, able to reply, able to imagine tomorrow.
I messaged Gotō: this is addiction, right? Withdrawal.
He replied: yes. Substance P governs not only anxiety but pain.
I put the phone face down on the table. Doudou barked once at the door.
Happiness is borrowed. Pain is what you pay back.
Two: A Week Later
I held out for a few days, then rewarded myself with one day.
That's my cycle: hold out, reward, low appetite, hold out again.
On reward day I'd buy a milk tea, order takeout, open the curtains, and feel I could pick my life back up.
The next day the drug wore off. I ate a few mouthfuls all day and didn't even want to wash Doudou's bowl.
In two months I lost almost ten jin. My waistband got loose, my cheekbones came out. Looking in the mirror, I thought the person there was thinner than me, and more of a stranger.
Mom asked if I'd lost weight. I said I was watching my diet. I knew I was lying to her.
Mom sent another voice message: come home for dinner this weekend. I said okay. I didn't tell her I was taking pills.
I have severe social anxiety. When I'm on pills, I can talk to someone online all night, and meeting them doesn't scare me;
when I'm not, I lie in bed, and whatever he says to me, all I can answer is 'mm', 'oh', 'ah', 'haha'. He says I seem autistic.
I know he doesn't mean it as an insult.
Last month I met up with someone I'd talked to a lot online. That day I took pills, went to the seaside with him, and said a lot.
The next day I hadn't taken anything. We lay in the hotel, and he asked what was wrong. I said nothing.
On the quitting forum I saw a PubMed case: a woman with no psychiatric history who took pregabalin for ten years for nerve pain,
and killed herself after stopping.
I screenshotted it and saved it. I didn't tell anyone I'd saved it.
I made up my mind to quit. But I don't know if I can. I don't want to call quitting a brave thing; it's just what I have to face tomorrow.
Today I put the pill box on the table and didn't open it.

beats.text: This loose page has no ending. She didn't say 'I quit', and she didn't say 'I took it again'. She just put the pill box on the table.

beats: I filed it in the 'unfinished' slot.

side-35.title: The Long Road
side-35.summary: Yuejin's log has no titles, only numbers.
beats: Yuejin's log has no titles, only numbers.
One: Still Working
Twenty-five
I added a little more. Not much, just a little. I wanted to get back the feeling from last time.
That night I turned off the room light and left only the phone screen. The fan turned overhead. I stared at the screen waiting for it to come on.
It came slowly, like a late train.
Twenty-six
It hit.
I told myself this time was just right. The music went slow, time went long. I woke the next day remembering nothing except 'it hit'.
Twenty-seven
I added a second time. Still scared, but I just wanted one big one again. A friend said don't add more. I said okay, then added more.
Twenty-eight
I couldn't sleep. I took something to force a shutdown, and it wouldn't shut down. I lay in bed hearing my own heartbeat, like someone knocking on the wall next door.
Twenty-nine
I woke very early. It was gone.
I stared at the ceiling and thought: where's my high?!
I thought it was just that one time wasn't enough.
Two: The High Is Gone
Thirty
I added again. Still nothing. Not 'weak' — nothing. Like pouring water into a cup with a hole in it.
I started logging 'how long until it hits'. Before it was an hour, then two, then I didn't know whether it had hit at all.
Thirty-one
I changed the time, the empty stomach, the order. Nothing worked. I thought it was tolerance, so I waited a few days. A few days later, the same.
Thirty-two
I added a lot. Threw up. The stomach acid was bitter. I added a little more.
Delirium. I think a stretch of memory was pulled out of me. I lay in bed, threw up all over it, forgot. I remember going to the mirage.
That night my head was a broken radio, every channel on at once. I heard someone call my name, and someone laughing.
I knew it was fake, but I still answered.
Thirty-three
I sat outside the supermarket. I thought, maybe I'll add a little more. A man in uniform chased me home. I got home and added more.
I sat on the edge of the bed feeling I was on a turntable. The turntable was huge, with wind. At most twenty-three floors high.
Two minutes later the turntable stopped, right on the chorus.
Thirty-four
I drank a bottle of grapefruit juice and started eating. Headache. Nausea. I swallowed for a long time. Then the dissociation came. My brain and I were two different people.
As soon as I sat up, my brain turned on its own; I couldn't control it. I felt I was going to die.
I kept sleeping. Extremely sensitive to music.
The last line is:
In the toilet, ugh, a smell of medicine.
And then nothing.

beats.text: This loose page doesn't close. Yuejin didn't write 'I quit', and didn't write 'I died'. The log stops at 'a smell of medicine'. The next page is blank.

beats: I filed it as it was, without writing anything in.

side-58.title: Master
beats: He called me master.
August 2023, he added me in the group for the first time. He said he'd read what I wrote and wanted to call me master.
I said don't. He said okay, then kept calling me that. The first time he called me master, I almost laughed. Later I got used to it.
The first photo he sent me was a bowl of noodles. The caption: Master, I ate today.
I replied 'good'.
After that he sent one every day. Sometimes noodles, sometimes a cat, sometimes his grandmother's balcony. Like clocking in.
He was older than me. He used to have a job; then the job was gone. Every day he took pregabalin and dextromethorphan, saying it made him feel he was still here.
He moved into his grandmother's place, living on money from who knows who. He told me, master, I'm not taking any today; the next day, master, I took some.
There was nothing I could do.
Sometimes he'd send a photo: a bowl of noodles, a cat, his grandmother's balcony. Ordinary things, as if proving he was still alive.
A week before he died he sent a balcony with a white shirt drying on it. I didn't reply.
Sometimes I replied, sometimes not. I thought there would still be tomorrow.
May 10, 2024, I learned by chance that he was dead.
The contact said: he told me living was pointless, then deleted all his friends and asked me to delete him too. He posted a few pictures in the group, so I called the police.
On the phone I told him to call 120 himself. He wouldn't. If I'd guessed a few hours earlier, maybe I could have saved him. Too late.
I couldn't save him at all. He refused to leave, refused treatment, refused work. The original purpose of the od was long gone;
he was already dead — only his body died on 2024.04.28.
The drugs took away his feelings about the world and walked him permanently into himself.
As I write this loose page there's an empty chair at the desk. It's where he used to sit when he came over. The chair is empty, and the bowl is empty.
The phone screen lit up. A message in the group. Not him.
I didn't go to the funeral. I didn't know what capacity I'd go in. His family doesn't know me; and I wasn't his master.
I put his report next to number 58. There's a line in it that stops me every time:
The drugs took away his feelings about the world and walked him permanently into himself.
Tell me, what should I do?

beats.text: This loose page has no answer. Gotō left the question on the paper and didn't answer it for himself. I put it next to number 58, without a note.

side-83.title: The Police Car at the Gate
side-83.summary: In March I o'd twenty times.
beats: One: Frame-Locked
In March I o'd twenty times.
I don't remember how it started. I only remember one day I added a little, and my vision locked frame rate, changing once a second. A few seconds later everything went black for a moment.
I sat on the bed talking nonsense and crying. In the end, with the last of my awareness, I had my guardian pin me to the bed and give me medicine.
Waking the next day, I didn't remember what I'd done. There were screenshots on my phone of things I'd bought while high. I bought another batch.
I had no awareness of it and no control. All through March I felt pushed along by something.
I knew it was wrong, but that 'knowing' was also inside the high — there one moment, gone the next. I checked the records. Twenty times.
I couldn't believe I could use at that rate.
In April I got gastroenteritis and threw up everything I ate. That calmed me down a bit. I got magnesium L-threonate and recovered a little from that long dissociation.
Right at the start of May, dextromethorphan moved to Schedule II. I thought I'd quit along with it. Then a few days ago I thought: one last o.
While high, I very unreasonably bought another batch, taking the risk.
Now, seeing what's written on the wiki, I understand: it was the dextro that took my judgment, and kept me from noticing.
I messaged Gotō: what am I supposed to do.
Someone in the group asked why I'd gone quiet. I said I was busy. Actually I was waiting for the high.
He replied: you have to recognize what's left of your life besides Umi.
I stared at that sentence for a long time. I couldn't think of an answer. I didn't even know what was left of 'my life';
I only knew that tomorrow the high would pass, I'd feel awful, and then I'd want it again.
Two: The Police Car
Today there's a police car parked at the entrance to the compound.
I went down to throw out the trash and saw it. My first thought: they're here for me. I stood in the stairwell and didn't go out. My heart raced; my palms sweated.
I remembered someone in the group saying checks were strict lately; I remembered the things I'd bought; I remembered the chat logs on my phone.
I told myself: is this persecutory delusion?
I didn't move. I stood behind the door and counted thirty seconds. Then I stuck my head out and looked.
The car was white, parked at the gate. The guard was sweeping. There was nobody in the car. A kid in a school uniform ran past it holding a grilled sausage.
It was just a car.
But I was shaking.
Replay · The Police Car at the Gate
This isn't a fight. It's a reality check.
- Rounds: 3.
- Hand (fixed, no deckbuilding): Breathe / Look out the window / Ask yourself / Message a friend.
- Opponent: Persecutory delusion.
- Opponent plays: shadow / footsteps / heartbeat.
- Goal: survive 3 rounds, and at the end choose 'look again'.
- No win or loss: psychology at zero = the delusion takes over the interpretation; the last line is still 'It was just a car', only in a different tone.
- Forbidden: sirens, real police incidents, police imagery, uniforms, pursuit.
Round One: Shadow. You play 'Breathe'. The shadow retreats behind the curtain.
Round Two: Footsteps. You play 'Look out the window'. The guard is sweeping, broom stroke by stroke.
Round Three: Heartbeat. You play 'Ask yourself'. You ask: 'Is this persecutory delusion?' Then you choose 'look again'.
It was just a car. But I was shaking.

beats.text: This loose page has no 'overcoming'. He just looked one more time. One more look is already hard.

side-84.title: The Diversity of Afterglow
beats: Handler's Notes
Report 84 is only a few lines. He calls it 'a kind of afterglow'.
He says that the day before, when he od'd, his heart raced, he sweated, he felt awful. The next day he woke with tinnitus, his five senses stretched.
He was happy all day, 'like a sound person', and it even lasted into the next day.
He also says he almost never dissociates. That 'light, floating' feeling he rarely gets, even after a lot. He's naturally sensitive, and his drug resistance is strange.
He sent me one line:
I always feel I'm awake, and the drug in my head turns into waves of slight numbness.
I read that three times.
He said another thing:
Once I od'd before the half-life had ended. The od itself was a bit uncomfortable — tachycardia, sweating.
But when I woke the next day: tinnitus, and my five senses felt expanded, extended.
I started building a theory: left-threonate is anti-dissociative, dextro is dissociative; their interaction might explain the afterglow.
The magnesium L-threonate let him 'feel a trace of afterglow'. Maybe the key is NMDA, or the sigma receptor, or the memory circuit.
Every explanation was just short.
I looked up left-threonate, dextro, the sigma receptor, memory circuits. Every one was just short.
If the afterglow is memory recovery + reversal of suicidal ideation + brief euphoria, then number 84 has euphoria, has expanded senses,
has the 'like a sound person' happiness; but he never mentions memory recovery, or the reversal of suicidal ideation. He almost never dissociates.
If the afterglow must pass through dissociation, then number 84 isn't the afterglow. But his experience is too similar.
He says on his first od he felt he'd touched something like it in childhood. He says it doesn't matter; it just left a deep memory.
He also says he has an unusual resistance to dissociation.
I meant to put him in the 'afterglow' column. But I couldn't find a column that would hold him.
He isn't memory recovery, isn't reversal of suicidal ideation, isn't the light after dissociation that I know.
He just woke the next day feeling the world had gotten bigger, feeling 'like a sound person'.
I even wondered whether, because he almost never dissociates, the afterglow grew into a different shape in him. But that's only a guess.
I wrote down: this isn't the afterglow I know.
Then I crossed out 'isn't' and changed it to 'isn't entirely'. In the end I crossed out the whole sentence and left only:
The afterglow has no recipe and no uniform shape.

beats.text: Number 84 isn't a counterexample, and isn't evidence. He's a person. I put his report next to the afterglow entry, and didn't stuff it into any table.
